1.definition: An Ottoman battlefield tactic: a defensive perimeter of baggage carts chained together, with field artillery and matchlock infantry firing from behind the barricade. It let troops break heavy cavalry charges.

The dynasty's own court name for itself, from Timur's title Guregen ("royal son-in-law," earned by marrying into Genghis Khan's line). The Mughals never called themselves "Mughal" — that was an outsiders' label. To their own chancery they were the Gurkani, the house of Timur.

Timur's honorific, meaning "royal son-in-law" in Mongol — the title he claimed by marrying a woman of Genghis Khan's lineage, since he was not himself a Genghisid and could not take the title of khan. The Mughal court name Gurkani derives directly from it.

2.definition: The Persian architect who designed Humayun's Tomb in Delhi in 1572. His Timurid-influenced design became the template for later Mughal architecture, including the Taj Mahal.

3.definition: The collected letters of the Naqshbandi Sufi reformer Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi, written in Persian — a sustained argument that Akbar's syncretism had carried the Mughal court into apostasy and that orthodox Sunni Islam needed to reassert itself. They became foundational texts of South Asian Sunni revivalism for the next four centuries.

4.definition: The Mughal governor of Bengal in whose confrontation Nur Jahan's first husband Sher Afgan was killed in 1607. A "koka" was a foster-brother of the emperor (raised with him by a shared wet-nurse), a relationship that carried enormous trust at the Mughal court; the circumstances of Sher Afgan's death have been argued over ever since.

4.term: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems

5.definition: An Italian who was at the Mughal court around the time the Taj Mahal was built. Some later European writers wrongly claimed he, not Mughal architects, designed it.
A Persian master goldsmith who served as chief jeweler at the Mughal court for decades, overseeing the precious-stone and metalwork on major imperial projects.

A medieval city founded by Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq in the 14th century, one of several successive cities built on the Delhi plain — the site on which Shah Jahan's city of Shahjahanabad was partially overlaid.

The persistent and false claim that the Taj Mahal was designed by a European — usually a Venetian or Frenchman named Geronimo Veroneo or Austin of Bordeaux. There is no contemporary evidence for it; the design is squarely in the Timurid-Persian garden-tomb tradition, and the chief named architect in Mughal sources is Ustad Ahmad Lahori. The myth is a colonial-era invention reluctant to credit Indo-Islamic builders.

6.definition: An Afghan chief whose life Dara Shikoh had once spared at personal cost — only for Malik Jiwan to hand the fugitive prince over to Aurangzeb's forces in 1659 in exchange for a reward, a notorious betrayal in the Mughal succession war.

The syncretist blending of Sufi (mystical Islamic) and Hindu Vedanta thought that Dara Shukoh pursued in his writings — the search for a shared mystical truth beneath the two traditions, expressed in his book the Majma-ul-Bahrain ("Confluence of the Two Seas"). Aurangzeb's clerics treated these very writings as the evidence of apostasy that justified Dara's execution.

The battle of February 1658 at which Dara Shukoh's army, led by his son Sulaiman Shikoh, defeated Shah Shuja's bid for the throne in the opening round of the Mughal war of succession. It was a victory that came to nothing: Dara would lose the decisive battle at Samugarh three months later, and Aurangzeb would take the throne.

9.definition: The Persian-language journal kept by the poet Mirza Ghalib recording the 1857 siege of Delhi and its brutal aftermath, which he lived through firsthand.

The cultural synthesis that emerged from centuries of Persian-speaking Islamic courts governing the Indian subcontinent — blending Persian administrative language, literature, and artistic conventions with indigenous Indian traditions. It defined the Mughal court's aesthetic and the broader urban Muslim culture of South Asia from the Sultanate period through the nineteenth century.

The collected Urdu poetry of Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, published under his poetic pen-name Zafar ("victory"). A genuine and respected body of work in the Urdu classical canon — the irony being that the emperor with the least real power left the most enduring literary legacy of the late dynasty.
